title: Scylla et Circe
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Glaucus crosses the Tyrrhenian sea to Circe's hall and asks her for a spell or a herb — not to cure his love for Scylla, but to make Scylla feel it too. Circe offers herself instead, and when he swears that leaves will grow in the open sea before his love changes, she poisons the pool where Scylla goes to escape the noon heat; Scylla wades in to the waist and finds that her thighs, shins and feet have become the jaws of barking dogs. Glaucus weeps and flees any marriage with Circe, and Scylla stays where she is, robbing Ulysses of his crew out of hatred for Circe and turning at last into the rock sailors still avoid.

sentences.t:
Iamque Giganteis iniectam faucibus Aetnen
arvaque Cyclopum, quid rastra, quid usus aratri
nescia nec quicquam iunctis debentia bubus,
liquerat Euboicus tumidarum cultor aquarum,
sentences.l: And now Etna, flung upon the Giant’s jaws, and the fields of the Cyclopes — fields knowing nothing of what harrows are, what the use of the plough is, and owing nothing to yoked oxen — the Euboean dweller in the swollen waters had left behind,
sentences.i: And by now the Euboean who makes his home in the swelling waters had left Etna behind him, flung down on the Giant’s jaws, and the Cyclopes’ fields, which know nothing of harrows or of what a plough is for and owe nothing to a yoke of oxen,
sentences.n: The sentence holds its verb and its subject back to the fourth line, so the reader passes a mountain and a whole countryside before learning who left them. Aetnen is the accusative in its Greek form, kept as Greek names are in Latin verse, and iniectam is the perfect participle of inicere agreeing with it: the mountain is the thing thrown, and Giganteis faucibus is the dative of what it was thrown on. The Giant is not named here. nescia is neuter plural agreeing with arva and governs two indirect questions, quid rastra and quid usus aratri, with the verb left out of both: “not knowing what harrows are, what the use of the plough is”. debentia is a second neuter plural participle on arva, and iunctis bubus is the dative of what the debt would be owed to — the yoked pair is the standard Latin unit of ploughing. The subject when it comes is cultor, the word for a tiller of soil, given here to a creature of water and set two lines below the fields that were never tilled — arva in line 2, cultor in line 4.

sentences.t:
liquerat et Zanclen adversaque moenia Rhegi
navifragumque fretum, gemino quod litore pressum
Ausoniae Siculaeque tenet confinia terrae.
sentences.l: he had left Zancle too, and the walls of Rhegium facing it, and the ship-wrecking strait which, pressed by a twin shore, holds the boundaries of the Ausonian and the Sicilian land.
sentences.i: he had left Zancle too, and the walls of Rhegium that face it across the water, and the ship-breaking strait which, squeezed between its two coasts, holds the frontier of Italy and Sicily.
sentences.n: liquerat stands as the first word of line 4 and again as the first word of line 5: the same verb at the head of two lines running, which is the figure called anaphora, and it is what lets the second line carry no subject of its own. navifragum is a compound built like a kenning, navis plus frangere, “ship-breaking”; Latin builds such compounds freely. quod is the relative with fretum as its antecedent, and pressum is a participle agreeing with it, gemino litore being the ablative of what does the pressing — one shore called twin rather than two shores, so the squeeze is written into the grammar. confinia is the noun for a shared border, and it takes both genitives, Ausoniae and Siculae terrae; Ausonia is an old poetic name for Italy. Zancle is the town on the Sicilian side of the strait, Rhegium the town facing it on the Italian side.

sentences.t:
Inde manu magna Tyrrhena per aequora raptus
herbiferos adiit colles atque atria Glaucus
Sole satae Circes, variarum plena ferarum.
sentences.l: From there, swept by a great hand through the Tyrrhenian levels, Glaucus came to the herb-bearing hills and the halls of Circe born of the Sun, halls full of beasts of every kind.
sentences.i: From there Glaucus was swept across the Tyrrhenian water by a great stroke of the arm and came to the herb-bearing hills and the hall of Circe, the Sun’s own daughter, a hall full of beasts of every kind.
sentences.n: raptus is a participle and manu magna the ablative of means. The Latin does not say whose hand: most naturally his own, a swimmer’s stroke rather than anyone else’s doing. herbiferos is the first word in the part to point at what Circe deals in, and it is put on the hills before the halls are reached. Sole satae is a participle from serere, “to sow”, in the genitive agreeing with Circes: “sown of the Sun” is the ordinary Latin way of saying whose child a person is, and Circes is the Greek genitive. plena is neuter plural and so agrees with atria, not with Circes — it is the halls that are full of animals, and variarum ferarum is the genitive that plena takes. Magnus prints raptus, “swept along”; some editions print vectus, “carried”, which makes the crossing an ordinary passage rather than a rush.

sentences.t:
Quam simul adspexit, dicta acceptaque salute,
“diva, dei miserere, precor!
sentences.l: And as soon as he caught sight of her, a greeting given and received, “Goddess, have pity on a god, I beg!”
sentences.i: The moment he set eyes on her, greetings given and returned: “Goddess, pity a god, I beg you!”
sentences.n: Quam is a connecting relative opening the sentence — it is Circe, in the accusative as the object of adspexit, and English wants a plain “her”. simul on its own does duty for simul ac, “as soon as”. dicta acceptaque salute is an ablative absolute with one noun and two participles hung on it, the compact Latin way of getting a whole scene of greeting into three words. miserere is the imperative of the deponent misereor and takes the genitive of the person pitied, dei. diva and dei stand side by side as the first two words he speaks: he is asking a goddess to pity a god, and the claim of equal rank is the first move of the request.

sentences.t:
nam sola levare
tu potes hunc,” dixit “videar modo dignior esse!
sentences.l: “for you alone are able to relieve this one here,” he said, “provided only that I seem to be worthy enough!”
sentences.i: “for you alone can give this man relief,” he said, “if only I can seem worthy enough!”
sentences.n: sola tu potes puts the pronoun after the adjective for emphasis: not “you can” but “you alone can”. hunc is Glaucus speaking of himself in the third person, picking up dei from the line before; he keeps the distance for one word more before dropping it. levare is to lighten a load rather than to cure. modo with the subjunctive videar is the restrictive “provided only that”, though the clause can also be read as a wish standing on its own, “only let me seem worthy” — the Latin does not settle which. dignior is a comparative with nothing expressed to compare it to, which in Latin means “worthy enough”. Magnus prints videar modo dignior esse, leaving open what he might be worthy of; some editions print videar modo dignus amorem, “worthy of love”, which supplies the very thing Magnus leaves unsaid.

sentences.t:
Quanta sit herbarum, Titani, potentia, nulli
quam mihi cognitius, qui sum mutatus ab illis.
sentences.l: “How great the power of herbs is, daughter of the Titan, is known to no one better than to me, who have been changed by them.”
sentences.i: “Nobody knows better than I do, daughter of the Titan, how much herbs can do — I who was changed by them.”
sentences.n: The indirect question quanta sit herbarum potentia is itself the subject of the sentence, and cognitius is a neuter comparative used of it: “how great the power of herbs is, is better known to no one”. nulli is the dative of the person the thing is known to, and quam mihi is what it is measured against. Titani is a vocative, Circe addressed by her descent rather than her name — and it flatters her with exactly the power he is about to ask her to use. qui sum mutatus ab illis is a relative clause with a perfect passive and ab illis as the ablative of agent: the herbs did it to him. He does not say here what he was changed from or into; the claim is only that he has been through it, which is his credential for asking.

sentences.t: Neve mei non nota tibi sit causa furoris:
sentences.l: “And so that the cause of my madness may not be unknown to you:”
sentences.i: “And so that you shall not be left in the dark about what has driven me mad:”
sentences.n: Neve introduces a negative purpose clause with the subjunctive sit — “and so that ... may not”. non nota is a double negative used as understatement: “not unknown” for “perfectly plain”, a figure Latin is fond of and which is politer than telling a goddess she is ignorant. mei and furoris are the two ends of one genitive phrase, and the whole of the rest of the clause, non nota tibi sit causa, is set between them, so the sentence keeps the word for his madness back to the very end. furor is the strong word: not love but derangement. The colon that closes the line is the edition’s, and everything after it is the explanation promised here.

sentences.t:
litore in Italico, Messenia moenia contra,
Scylla mihi visa est;
sentences.l: “on the Italian shore, opposite the Messenian walls, Scylla was seen by me;”
sentences.i: “on the Italian shore, across from the walls of Messana, I caught sight of Scylla;”
sentences.n: Two prepositions in one line stand after the words they belong with: in comes between litore and Italico rather than in front of the phrase, and contra follows Messenia moenia entirely. Putting a preposition behind its noun is called anastrophe and is a mark of high verse. Scylla mihi visa est can be taken two ways and the Latin does not choose: mihi as a dative of the agent with the passive visa est, “Scylla was seen by me”, or the ordinary dative with videor in its other sense, “Scylla appeared to me”. The literal here takes the first. Messana is the Roman name of the town called Zancle at line 5, so he is standing on the Italian side of the same strait the part opened with.

sentences.t:
pudor est promissa precesque
blanditiasque meas contemptaque verba referre.
sentences.l: “it is a shame to relate my promises and prayers and coaxings, and the words that were treated with contempt.”
sentences.i: “I am ashamed to repeat the promises, the pleading, the sweet talk of mine — and the words she despised.”
sentences.n: pudor est with an infinitive is impersonal: it is a shame to do the thing, with referre as the subject of est and the four accusatives as its objects. The three -que endings string the list together without a pause, and meas agrees only with blanditias although it colours the whole run. blanditiae are coaxing, wheedling words, the vocabulary of a lover. contempta is a participle and it is the only place in his account where the refusal is stated at all: he never says outright that she said no, and the whole of it is folded into one adjective on his own words. He is telling Circe he was rejected while declining to describe the rejection.

sentences.t:
At tu, sive aliquod regnum est in carmine, carmen
ore move sacro, sive expugnantior herba est,
utere temptatis operosae viribus herbae.
sentences.l: “But you: if there is any sovereignty in a spell, set a spell moving with your holy mouth; or if the herb is the better stormer of walls, use the tried strengths of the herb that labours.”
sentences.i: “But you — if a spell holds any power, then let your holy mouth set the spell going; or if the herb is better at storming the walls, use the proven strength of the herb that does the work.”
sentences.n: sive ... sive offers her a choice of instrument, spell or herb, and he leaves the choice to her. carmine and carmen stand side by side with only a comma between them, and carmen closes line 20: the same word twice over in two cases, so the ablative of the condition hands straight over to the accusative of the command. move is the imperative: a carmen is set in motion rather than spoken. expugnantior is a comparative built on a present participle, “more taking-by-storm”; expugnare is the verb for carrying a town by assault, and the language of siege warfare is being used of a love-charm. utere is the imperative of the deponent utor and takes the ablative viribus, with temptatis meaning powers already put to the test. operosae herbae is a genitive: operosus is “full of work”, said either of a thing that costs effort or of one that gets things done.

sentences.t:
Nec medeare mihi sanesque haec vulnera mando,
fineque nil opus est:
sentences.l: “And I do not charge you that you doctor me and make these wounds sound, and of an ending there is no need:”
sentences.i: “And I am not asking you to cure me, or to close these wounds; I have no need of an ending:”
sentences.n: mando governs two bare subjunctives, medeare and sanes, with no ut between: this is the ordinary way verse reports a command, and English has to supply a “that”. medeare is the shortened second person of the deponent medeor and takes the dative mihi. nec negatives the whole of mando and so both subjunctives with it. opus est takes the ablative of the thing needed, fine, and nil is an accusative used adverbially, “in no respect”. The turn is the point of the whole speech: he does not ask to be cured, and refuses the cure in advance.

sentences.t: partem ferat illa caloris.”
sentences.l: “let her carry a share of the heat.”
sentences.i: “let her take her share of the fire.”
sentences.n: ferat is a jussive subjunctive standing on its own, with no verb of asking in front of it: “let her carry”. illa is Scylla, who has not been named since line 18. calor is heat, the standing Latin metaphor for desire, and partem caloris makes it a quantity that can be divided — he does not want less of it himself, he wants her to have some. Four words carry the whole request, and they are what Circe will act on: he has asked for a spell that will make another woman burn.

sentences.t:
At Circe (neque enim flammis habet aptius ulla
talibus ingenium, seu causa est huius in ipsa,
seu Venus indicio facit hoc offensa paterno)
talia verba refert.
sentences.l: But Circe (for no woman has a temper better fitted to such flames, whether the cause of this lies in her own self, or whether Venus, offended by a father’s informing, makes it so) returns such words as these.
sentences.i: But Circe — no woman has a nature readier to take such fire, whether the reason for it lies in herself or whether Venus, offended by the way Circe’s father informed on her, brings it about — gives him back an answer like this.
sentences.n: The parenthesis opens two words into line 25 and closes at the end of line 27, and the poem puts its own explanation of Circe inside it before letting her speak. ulla is feminine with no noun, “any woman”. aptius is a comparative on ingenium with the dative flammis talibus: a temper better suited to catching fire. seu ... seu sets out two causes and settles neither, and huius is a genitive, “the cause of this”. offensa agrees with Venus and takes the ablative of what gave the offence, indicio paterno, where the adjective “paternal” does the work of a genitive. The father is Circe’s, not Venus’s: the informer is the Sun, and the English has to say so, because in English “her father” would be read of Venus. The Latin does not say what was informed of; the standing story is that the Sun told what he had seen of Venus. refert is “carries back”, the verb for an answer returned.

sentences.t:
“Melius sequerere volentem
optantemque eadem parilique cupidine captam.
sentences.l: “You would do better to follow a woman who is willing and who wants the same things, one caught by a desire to match.”
sentences.i: “You would do better to chase a woman who is willing — one who wants the same thing, taken by a longing equal to your own.”
sentences.n: sequerere is the shortened form of sequereris, the imperfect subjunctive of the deponent sequor, used as a potential: “you would do better to follow”, a suggestion rather than a statement about what he did. volentem, optantem and captam are three feminine accusative participles with no noun anywhere for them to belong to — the woman is described and never named, and Circe is describing herself while keeping the third person. eadem is neuter plural, the object of optantem: the same things he wants. parili cupidine is the ablative with captam, and capere of desire is the ordinary metaphor of being taken prisoner. Her whole argument is contained in the participles: willing, wanting, already caught.

sentences.t:
Dignus eras ultro (poteras certeque) rogari,
et, si spem dederis, mihi crede, rogaberis ultro.
sentences.l: “You were worthy to be asked without asking (and certainly you could have been), and, if you give hope, believe me, you will be asked without asking.”
sentences.i: “You deserved to be asked without ever having to ask — and you certainly could have been; and if you offer any hope, take my word for it, you will be asked.”
sentences.n: dignus with a passive infinitive, rogari, is a poetic construction where prose would use a relative clause with the subjunctive. ultro is the word for doing a thing unprompted, and it stands in both lines, closing the second: it is the pivot of her offer, since he has been the one begging and she is telling him he ought to be the one begged. poteras is a plain imperfect indicative where English wants “could have been” — Latin regularly uses the indicative of posse for a possibility that was never taken up — and the -que of certeque joins the parenthesis to what precedes rather than sitting where English would put “and”. dederis is a future perfect in the if-clause with the plain future rogaberis in the main clause, the ordinary Latin sequence that English flattens into a present. mihi crede is a two-word command dropped into the middle of the sentence, “believe me”.

sentences.t: Neu dubites adsitque tuae fiducia formae:
sentences.l: “And do not hesitate, and let confidence in your own beauty be at hand:”
sentences.i: “And do not hang back — let there be confidence in your own good looks:”
sentences.n: Neu is a shortened neve, introducing a negative command with the subjunctive dubites, and adsit is a jussive subjunctive joined to it by -que. tuae formae is an objective genitive with fiducia: confidence placed in your beauty, not confidence belonging to it. Magnus prints adsitque, “and let confidence be there”; some editions print absitque, “and let confidence be absent”, which reverses the sentence into a warning not to presume on his looks. The line reads as encouragement in Magnus and as a rebuke in the other reading, and the two are only one letter apart.

sentences.l: “Look at me: though I am a goddess, though the daughter of the shining Sun, though I can do so much by grass and so much by song as well, I vow that I may be yours;”
sentences.i: “Look at me: goddess though I am, daughter of the shining Sun, able to do so much with a herb and just as much with a spell — I vow myself yours;”
sentences.n: en points at her, and the speech turns here from what he deserves to what she is. There are three cum clauses with the subjunctive, sim and possim, all of them concessive — “although I am” — and the second has no verb of its own but borrows sim from the first. Each names a reason she should be above asking, and the sentence spends all three on the vow at the end. gramine and carmine are ablatives of means, and the repeated tantum ... tantum balances her two kinds of power, the herb and the spell — the same pair Glaucus had offered her the choice of at lines 20 to 22. quoque here is the adverb “also” and not quo-que, “and by which”. voveo is the verb for making a vow to a god, and it takes the ut clause as its content: she is not promising herself to him so much as dedicating herself, in the language of an offering.

sentences.t:
spernentem sperne, sequenti
redde vices unoque duas ulciscere facto!”
sentences.l: “scorn the woman who scorns, pay back like for like to the woman who follows, and with one act avenge two!”
sentences.i: “scorn the one who scorns you, give the one who follows you what she gives, and with one act avenge two women!”
sentences.n: spernentem and sequenti are participles used as nouns, both feminine and neither named: the one who scorns is Scylla, the one who follows is Circe herself, who has already said en ego two lines earlier and now goes back to describing herself from the outside. redde vices is the standing phrase for paying like with like, vices being the turns of an exchange. ulciscere is the imperative of the deponent ulciscor, active in meaning although its ending is not the shape of one. duas is feminine, so the two are women — most simply Scylla scorned and Circe answered. What is left bare is what the one verb does for each: ulcisci cannot mean quite the same thing for both, since one is to be punished and the other satisfied. The Latin compresses, and the compression is what makes the line quotable.

sentences.t:
Talia temptanti “prius” inquit “in aequore frondes”
Glaucus “et in summis nascentur montibus algae,
sospite quam Scylla nostri mutentur amores!”
sentences.l: To her as she tried such things Glaucus said: “Sooner shall leaves grow in the open sea, and seaweed on the mountain tops, than my love be changed, with Scylla living safe!”
sentences.i: To this attempt of hers Glaucus said: “Leaves will grow in the open sea, and seaweed on the mountain tops, before ever my love changes while Scylla is alive and safe!”
sentences.n: Talia temptanti is a dative participle standing as a noun with no pronoun anywhere for “her”: “to the one attempting such things”. The edition closes the quotation at the end of line 37 and opens it again after Glaucus in line 38, because the speaker’s name cuts across the speech; the name arrives a whole line after inquit, which is the verse trick of putting the interruption where it hurts most. prius in line 37 waits for its quam, which is the second word of line 39. mutentur is subjunctive after priusquam, the mood Latin uses when the clause names something the speaker means to prevent. sospite Scylla is an ablative absolute made of an adjective and a noun with no participle at all: Latin has no present participle of esse to put in, so this is how it says “while Scylla is safe”. nostri amores is a poetic plural for a single love, and nostri stands for mei. The oath is an adynaton — an impossibility named so that the refusal cannot be argued with.

sentences.t:
Indignata dea est, et laedere quatenus ipsum
non poterat (nec vellet amans), irascitur illi,
quae sibi praelata est,
sentences.l: The goddess was indignant, and since she could not harm him himself — nor, being in love, would she have wished to — she turns her anger on the woman who was preferred to her,
sentences.i: The goddess was outraged; and since she could not hurt him, and in love as she was would not have wanted to, she turns her rage on the woman who had been preferred to her,
sentences.n: Indignata est is the perfect of the deponent indignor, active in meaning. quatenus here is causal, “seeing that”, not the local “as far as”, and it is held back behind the infinitive laedere that its clause governs. poterat is imperfect indicative, a plain statement of what was not possible, while vellet beside it is subjunctive, the unreal “would not have wished”: two moods in one breath, separating what she could not do from what she never wanted to. amans is a participle doing the work of a whole clause, “because she was in love”. irascitur is a present dropped into a past narrative — the historic present, and it arrives exactly with the anger; it takes the dative illi. praelata est is the perfect passive of praeferre with sibi as the dative of the person passed over. Scylla is not named in these lines; she is only “that woman, who”.

sentences.t:
venerisque offensa repulsa
protinus horrendis infamia pabula sucis
conterit et tritis Hecateia carmina miscet
caerulaque induitur velamina perque ferarum
agmen adulantum media procedit ab aula,
sentences.l: and, offended by the rejection of her love, she at once grinds together ill-famed fodder with dreadful juices, and to the ground stuff mixes in the songs of Hecate, and clothes herself in dark-blue veils, and through the throng of fawning wild beasts comes out from the middle of her hall,
sentences.i: and, stung by the rebuff her love had met, she grinds up at once a mash of plants of evil name with dreadful juices, works the spells of Hecate into the grindings, wraps herself in dark-blue veils, and comes out from the middle of her hall through the fawning press of wild beasts,
sentences.n: repulsa is the noun for a rejection — properly the word for losing an election — and veneris is an objective genitive: the love she offered was the thing rejected. offensa agrees with Circe and takes the ablative of what gave offence. pabulum is fodder, what an animal is put to eat, so the plants are named by what they are for and not by what they are; infamia is “of evil name”. conterit and tritis stand in the same line, 44: the compound first and then the simple verb it is built on, tero, in its participle — the grinding and then the ground stuff, and the literal keeps the repetition. Hecate is the goddess of witchcraft and of crossroads, and Hecateia carmina are spells that belong to her. induitur is passive in form but reflexive in sense — she puts the veils on herself — and it keeps its accusative object velamina, which is the clue to the use. adulantum is the shortened genitive plural of adulantium, the word used of dogs fawning; these are the beasts the part put in her halls at line 10, and dogs are about to matter a great deal. media ... ab aula is “from the middle of the hall”.

sentences.t:
oppositumque petens contra Zancleia saxa
Rhegion ingreditur ferventes aestibus undas,
in quibus ut solida ponit vestigia terra
summaque decurrit pedibus super aequora siccis.
sentences.l: and making for Rhegium, which lies opposite over against the Zanclean rocks, she steps into waves boiling with tides, on which she sets her footprints as on solid ground and runs across the surface of the sea with dry feet.
sentences.i: and making for Rhegium, which lies across the water facing the rocks of Zancle, she steps out onto waves that boil with the tide, plants her feet on them as though on hard ground, and runs over the top of the sea dry-shod.
sentences.n: oppositumque opens line 47 and Rhegion opens line 48, with petens contra Zancleia saxa standing between the adjective and the noun it belongs to. Rhegion keeps its Greek ending in the accusative. ingreditur is a deponent, active in meaning, and takes a direct object in the accusative, undas. aestus means both a boiling heat and the run of the tide, and ferventes plays on the pair — the strait is famous for its race. ut with the ablative solida terra is “as on solid ground”, with the verb left out. summa aequora is not the whole sea but the top of it: summus of a thing means its surface or its highest part. In line 50 siccis is held back to the very end, with super aequora standing between it and pedibus, so the dry feet are the last thing the sentence says.

sentences.t:
Parvus erat gurges, curvos sinuatus in arcus,
grata quies Scyllae;
sentences.l: There was a small pool, curved into bending bows, a rest welcome to Scylla;
sentences.i: There was a little pool, curled into bending arcs — Scylla’s own quiet place;
sentences.n: gurges is properly a whirlpool or a deep place in a river; here it is a small still inlet, and the word is masculine, which matters four lines later. sinuatus is a participle agreeing with it, and in curvos arcus is the accusative with in for the shape a thing is bent into. grata quies Scyllae stands in apposition with no verb of its own: the pool is named and then named again by what it is for. quies is rest, the state, used here for the place where it is had, and Scyllae can be read as the dative that grata naturally takes or as a genitive of possession, the form being the same. The description is unhurried and dwells on the place, which is how the poem sets a trap.

sentences.t:
quo se referebat ab aestu
et maris et caeli, medio cum plurimus orbe
sol erat et minimas a vertice fecerat umbras.
sentences.l: to which she used to take herself back from the heat both of the sea and of the sky, when the sun was at its fullest in the middle of its circuit and had made the shadows smallest from the point overhead.
sentences.i: where she would retreat from the heat of sea and sky alike, at the hour when the sun stood at its highest in mid-course and cast the shortest shadows from the zenith.
sentences.n: quo is a connecting relative of place, “to which”, and referebat is an imperfect of habit: this is what she used to do, not what she did once. aestus here is heat, the other of the two senses the same word carried at line 48. et ... et is “both ... and”. plurimus is an adjective where English wants an adverb — the sun at its most — and medio orbe is the ablative of where in its circuit it stands. cum with the indicative erat is the plain temporal “when”, not the narrative cum that takes a subjunctive. a vertice is “from the point directly above”. The cum clause spends the better part of two lines saying only “at midday”, and the poem takes its time because it is telling the reader exactly when Scylla will come.

sentences.t:
Hunc dea praevitiat portentificisque venenis
inquinat, hic pressos latices radice nocenti
spargit et obscurum verborum ambage novorum
ter noviens carmen magico demurmurat ore.
sentences.l: This the goddess spoils beforehand and fouls with monster-making poisons; here she sprinkles juices pressed from a hurtful root, and thrice nine times mutters through, with magic mouth, a spell made dark by a winding of unheard-of words.
sentences.i: The goddess poisons the pool in advance and fouls it with venoms that breed monsters; here she sprinkles the sap squeezed from a harmful root, and twenty-seven times mutters right through, with a magician’s mouth, a spell darkened by a winding of words nobody has heard.
sentences.n: hunc must be the pool, gurges at line 51, although two nearer masculine nouns stand between, aestu at 52 and sol at 54: only the sense decides it. praevitiat is a compound: vitiare is to spoil or corrupt, and the prefix says she does it before the victim arrives, which is the whole method of the ambush. portentificis is another compound, “making portents”, and it is the first hint of what shape the poison will take. latex is any liquid, here the sap forced out of the root, and radice nocenti is the ablative of source. obscurum stands in line 57 and its noun carmen in line 58, with the ablative phrase and the count of repetitions set between them; verborum and novorum in the same way stand on either side of ambage. ambages is a winding or a roundabout way of speaking. ter noviens is “three times nine”, twenty-seven, magic counting in threes. demurmurat is murmurare with de- on it: to mutter a thing right through, under the breath.

sentences.t:
Scylla venit mediaque tenus descenderat alvo,
cum sua foedari latrantibus inguina monstris
adspicit ac primo credens non corporis illas
esse sui partes refugitque abigitque timetque
ora proterva canum,
sentences.l: Scylla came, and had gone down as far as the middle of her belly, when she sees her own loins being fouled with barking monsters; and at first, believing that those are not parts of her own body, she shrinks back and drives them off and is afraid of the shameless mouths of the dogs,
sentences.i: Scylla came, and had waded in as far as the waist, when she catches sight of her own loins being fouled with barking monsters; and at first, believing that they are no part of her own body, she recoils, beats them away, is frightened of the brazen mouths of the dogs,
sentences.n: tenus is a postposition and stands after the ablative it governs, media alvo: the water is at her waist, which is exactly where the change will cut her. The cum clause is the inverted kind — the main clause carries the background and the cum clause carries the event — so English has to turn it round into “she had gone in ... when she saw”. foedari is a present infinitive in indirect statement after adspicit, with sua inguina as its subject accusative: she sees them being fouled, in the act of it. credens introduces a second indirect statement, this one negative, and corporis, next to last in line 61, is separated from its sui in line 62 by illas and esse, so her own body is held apart in the word order at the moment she refuses to own it. refugit, abigit and timet are three verbs strung with -que and no pause; refugit could be a perfect on its form alone, but the two beside it are unambiguously present, so all three are the historic present, arriving with the horror. protervus is the word for shameless forwardness in a person, and given to dogs’ mouths it makes them behave like an insolent crowd.

sentences.t:
sed quos fugit, attrahit una
et corpus quaerens femorum crurumque pedumque,
Cerbereos rictus pro partibus invenit illis:
sentences.l: but the ones she flees she drags along together with her; and seeking the substance of her thighs and shins and feet, she finds Cerberus-gapes in place of those parts:
sentences.i: but the ones she runs from she drags along with her; and looking for the body of her thighs, her shins, her feet, she finds gaping Cerberus-mouths where those parts should be:
sentences.n: quos has no antecedent expressed and stands for the dogs named a few words earlier in this same line 63, canum; its clause comes in front of the verb it depends on. una is the adverb “together”, not the numeral: what she runs from runs with her, because it is fastened to her. corpus here is not the body entire but the bodily substance of the parts just named, and the three genitives femorum crurumque pedumque run down the leg in order, thigh to shin to foot, so that the search is made in the word order. rictus is the open gape of a mouth rather than the mouth itself. Cerbereos names Cerberus, the dog of the underworld, and the adjective does the work of a comparison. pro partibus illis is a plain preposition doing the whole of the transformation: in place of those parts. The colon at the end of the line is the edition’s, and the two lines after it are the result.

sentences.t:
statque canum rabie subiectaque terga ferarum
inguinibus truncis uteroque exstante coercet.
sentences.l: and she stands on a madness of dogs, and with loins cut short and belly jutting out she pens in the backs of the beasts set beneath her.
sentences.i: and she stands upon a rage of dogs, holding the backs of the beasts down beneath her with her docked loins and jutting belly.
sentences.n: stat with the ablative rabie is “stands on”, and what she stands on is not the dogs but their madness: the abstract noun is put where the animals should be, and that is the point of the line. subiecta terga is from subicere, to throw underneath — the backs are the beasts’, placed under her. inguinibus truncis and uteroque exstante are two ablatives, most simply of means, naming what she holds them down with; they can also be read as ablative absolutes describing her state, and the Latin does not choose between the two. truncus is the word for something lopped, a tree with the limbs cut off. coercet is the verb for fencing a thing in or keeping a crowd in order, and it leaves her holding herself together.

sentences.t:
Flevit amans Glaucus nimiumque hostiliter usae
viribus herbarum fugit conubia Circes;
sentences.l: Glaucus wept as a lover, and fled marriage with Circe, who had used the powers of herbs all too much in the manner of an enemy;
sentences.i: Glaucus wept as a lover weeps, and fled any marriage with Circe, who had used the strength of her herbs far too much as an enemy would;
sentences.n: amans is a participle used as a noun, “as a lover”, and it is the same word the poem gave to Circe at line 41: the two of them are labelled alike, and only one of them acted on it. usae is the perfect participle of the deponent utor in the genitive feminine agreeing with Circes, with viribus herbarum as the ablative it governs — a whole clause folded into one word, and it comes before the name it belongs to. Circes is the Greek genitive. hostiliter is the adverb from hostis, an enemy in war rather than a personal foe, and nimium measures it: not that she was cruel but that she fought, and fought too hard. conubia is a poetic plural for a single marriage. The line does not say whom he was still in love with, and the Latin leaves it standing open.

sentences.t:
Scylla loco mansit cumque est data copia primum,
in Circes odium sociis spoliavit Ulixen;
sentences.l: Scylla stayed in that place, and as soon as the chance was first given, out of hatred towards Circe she stripped Ulysses of his companions;
sentences.i: Scylla stayed where she was, and at the first chance she got she robbed Ulysses of his crew, to spite Circe;
sentences.n: loco is a bare ablative of place with no preposition, which verse allows where prose would want in. cum primum, “as soon as”, is pulled apart, with est data copia standing between the two words. est data is passive with nobody named as giving the chance. in Circes odium is in with the accusative of a feeling, the construction for “to the hurt of”, “out of hatred towards”: the hatred is owed to Circe and the men who pay for it are Ulysses’s. spoliavit takes the person robbed in the accusative and the thing taken away in the ablative, so sociis ... Ulixen is “Ulysses, of his companions”, and the men are grammatically the property rather than the victims. Ulixen keeps its Greek ending in the accusative where Latin would have Ulixem.

sentences.t:
mox eadem Teucras fuerat mersura carinas,
ni prius in scopulum, qui nunc quoque saxeus exstat,
transformata foret:
sentences.l: soon the same woman would have sunk the Trojan keels, had she not first been turned into a crag, which even now stands out in stone:
sentences.i: soon she would have sent the Trojan ships to the bottom too, had she not first been turned into a reef — which juts up in stone to this day:
sentences.n: fuerat mersura is a future participle with the pluperfect of esse, the periphrasis Latin uses for what was on the point of happening and did not: “she was going to sink them”. Paired with ni ... foret it makes a past unreal condition, and the indicative fuerat standing beside the subjunctive foret is regular in that pattern; foret is the old form of esset. eadem, “the same woman”, is the only word carrying her over from the sentence before, and she is not named again in the rest of the part. Teucer was an ancestral king of Troy, so Teucras is “Trojan”, and carina is the keel put for the whole ship. in scopulum with transformata is in with the accusative for what a thing is turned into. quoque here is the adverb “even, also”, not quo-que; and nunc reaches out of the story into the reader’s own present.

sentences.t: scopulum quoque navita vitat.
sentences.l: the sailor avoids the crag too.
sentences.i: and sailors give the rock a wide berth as well.
sentences.n: scopulum is repeated from line 73, and here it is the first word of the clause that closes the part: the rock is said twice, and it is the only thing left of her. quoque is again the adverb, “as well”: she was avoided as a monster and she is avoided as a stone, so nothing has changed for the sailors and everything has changed for her. navita is the poetic form of nauta, singular for the whole class of them. vitat is present, and the tense carries the story out of myth and into the time of whoever is reading it — the same move nunc made in the line before.
